title: Land to those who work it
hook: Banda breaks the big estates and gives land to the farmers who tilled it

segments.voice: Yesterday, coins struck at Lohgarh with the Gurus' names where a ruler's own name would go. Your line was in their names. Whose name did you give credit to? Today, from coins to soil. Day eight hundred forty-two.

Two people stand at the edge of a field. One has mud to the knees; he plowed it, sowed it, and will cut it at harvest. The other has clean hands and a paper that says the field is his, and when the grain comes in, he takes the larger share. Tradition remembers that in Banda Singh's Punjab, land often worked that way. Big landholders collected, and the people who did the work kept what was left. Sikh tradition remembers that where Banda Singh's rule reached, he turned that around. Today: land to those who work it.
screen: `MUD TO THE KNEES.` → `CLEAN HANDS AND A PAPER.` → `BANDA SINGH TURNS IT AROUND.`

segments.voice: Tradition says Banda Singh broke up the big estates in the lands he held and gave the fields to the farmers who actually tilled them. Accounts differ on how far and how long this reached; he held those lands only for a time, under constant attack. But the idea is the part Sikhs keep. To hear where it comes from, go back to the very start of the path, to Guru Nanak. Sikh tradition tells of Guru Nanak staying with a carpenter named Bhai Lalo, a poor man who earned his bread by his own hands. A rich official, Malik Bhago, held a great feast and expected the holy man to come. Guru Nanak stayed with Lalo's plain bread. In the story, when the Guru is pressed to explain, he holds Lalo's coarse bread in one hand and Malik Bhago's rich food in the other and squeezes them. From Lalo's bread comes milk. From the feast, blood, because it was gathered from other people's labor. The Sikh word for that honest labor is kirat. Kirat karni, earning by honest work, is a pillar of Sikh life, taught beside remembering the Name and sharing. Banda Singh's land grants take that story out of a kitchen and into whole villages. The bread belongs with the hands that made it. The field belongs with the hands that work it. Some readers hear a modern echo in it, whenever people argue about who should own the fields they farm. But at its root, the idea is just a carpenter's bread, held up against a feast.
screen: `BIG ESTATES BROKEN UP.` · `LALO'S BREAD AND MALIK BHAGO'S FEAST.` · `KIRAT: EARNING BY HONEST WORK.` · `THE FIELD BELONGS WITH THE HANDS.` · then, large: `LAND TO THE TILLERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank a farmer. Sit, and let the breath settle. Think of the last thing you ate. Trace it backward, one step at a time: the shop, the truck, the packing shed, and finally a field somewhere, and a person bent over it in the heat or the cold. You'll probably never know their name. Hold them in mind anyway, with their tired back and their dirty hands. Let a simple thank you rise toward them. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out, and remember the hands behind your bread. The bell holds the time.
kirat, honest work. Banda Singh's breaking of the big estates, giving fields to the farmers who tilled them, rooted in Guru Nanak's honor for earning by one's own hands. Today's word.
Your line: land to the tillers. Today, at one meal, pause before the first bite and thank the hands that grew it. Day eight hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Banda Singh Bahadur for giving land to the farmers who tilled it, and connect it to Guru Nanak's teaching of kirat karni, earning by honest work, told in the story of Bhai Lalo and Malik Bhago.

Banda Singh's abolition of zamindari / grants to tillers: widely told; extent and duration debated. Confirm framing.
The Lalo and Malik Bhago story (milk and blood) is a janamsakhi tradition; confirm it appears in Macauliffe vol. 1 as cited.
'A pillar of Sikh life, taught beside remembering the Name and sharing' (naam japna, kirat karni, vand chhakna): confirm.
